summary:
Zenith turns open NASA Earth-observation data into honest, plain-language answers about a changing climate. 
For the US West Coast (Alaska, California, Hawaii, Oregon, and Washington), it measures trends in five variables: air temperature, precipitation, summer smoke, total water storage, and soil moisture. 
Every trend comes with a 95% confidence range and a significance verdict alongside the number itself. 
It fits trends together with the seasonal cycle and uses an autocorrelation-adjusted effective sample size (the correction the IPCC uses), so it never mistakes year-to-year noise for a real signal. 
A correlation engine finds which variables move together and states that a link is “consistent with A influencing B” only when a known physical mechanism fits. It never claims causation. 
A 2050 projection with an uncertainty band, an interactive map, and a “Try it anywhere on Earth” mode round it out. 
The engine was validated against 25 published studies (24 matched). 
This addresses the challenge by making NASA’s data interpretable, trustworthy, and accessible to non-experts and researchers alike.
details:
1. What does it do / how does it work? What benefits?
Zenith ingests monthly NASA satellite and model products, averages each over true US Census state outlines, then fits a straight-line trend jointly with the seasonal cycle. Significance uses an effective sample size derived from lag-1 autocorrelation (Santer et al. 2008 / IPCC AR6), which produces an honest 95% range and p-value. A trend is called “clear” only if it is significant and a robust Theil-Sen slope agrees. Otherwise the verdict is “no clear trend yet.” A separate correlation engine deseasonalizes and detrends the data, tests lagged relationships with false-discovery control and surrogate testing, and elevates a pair to “consistent with influence” only when a fixed table of 30 physical mechanisms fits. Benefits: anyone can see what is changing and how certain it is, without specialist tools. Researchers get auditable, reproducible methods and can test any region on Earth.

2. Intended impact:
Zenith makes NASA’s open climate record legible and trustworthy. Students and teachers get a working lesson in statistical significance, journalists get defensible numbers with ranges, local planners get state-level context, and researchers get a validated, reproducible engine they can extend. The deeper impact is cultural: showing uncertainty honestly and refusing to overclaim causation, which counters the climate misinformation that thrives on cherry-picked short trends.

3. Tools, languages, hardware, software:

  • Front end: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript; Chart.js (visualizations); Leaflet (maps). Static site hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Data pipeline: Python (numpy, pandas, xarray, scipy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, regionmask, geopandas, earthaccess, harmony-py), served via FastAPI for the “Try it” engine.
  • Data access: NASA Earthdata (Harmony subsetting, Giovanni averaging).
  • Statistics from libraries: Granger causality tests and Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery control come from statsmodels; the Hamed-Rao Mann-Kendall check (shown, never used to decide a verdict) comes from pymannkendall.
  • Hardware: Standard Laptop

4. How is it creative?
Most climate tools either dump raw data or over-simplify. Zenith’s novelty is making uncertainty and honesty first-class features. Every chart carries a confidence range and a plain-English verdict, and faded colours and patterns mark “not yet significant.” AI-written summaries are constrained to restate only computed numbers, and a checker rejects invented figures or causal language, with a template fallback. The physics-grounded correlation engine that refuses to say “causes,” and a “test any box on Earth” mode running the identical pipeline, make it both rigorous and genuinely usable.
